items.title: Sodium burns to make table salt — and then keeps wanting to react
items.claim: Sodium chloride formation looks like the textbook ionic reaction. Yet ionising Na to Na+ (+496 kJ/mol) and adding electron to Cl (-349 kJ/mol) gives a net cost of +147 kJ/mol. Why does it happen at all?
items.prompt: Where does the energy come from?

options.text: From the heat of the burning reaction
The lattice enthalpy — the enormous release of energy when Na+ and Cl- assemble into the crystal (around minus 787 kJ/mol) — dwarfs the cost of making the ions
From nowhere — the reaction is technically not spontaneous

items.reveal:
The full Born-Haber cycle for NaCl: atomise Na (+107), atomise Cl (+122), ionise Na (+496), add electron to Cl (-349), assemble lattice (-787). Net: -411 kJ/mol — exothermic and spontaneous.

Ionic bonding is NOT 'Na giving an electron to Cl' as the simple GCSE diagram suggests. It's the electrostatic stabilisation of a 3D crystal lattice. Lose the lattice (e.g., dissolve in water), and the bond is gone. NaCl(s) is stable; isolated NaCl molecules barely exist outside the gas phase.
items.why: The dot-and-cross diagram hides the energetics. Lattice enthalpy is where ionic compounds get their stability.

items.title: A blacksmith's anvil works because of heat capacity, not strength
items.claim: A 100 kg steel anvil sits cold under a 1300°C glowing iron bar. The bar bends; the anvil doesn't even warm to the touch. The mass of the anvil sets the rate at which the bar cools — but each strike still leaves the anvil cool.
items.prompt: Why doesn't the heat 'flow' into the anvil and damage it?

options.text: Heat flow is finite over the brief contact time; the anvil's large heat capacity buffers any small heat input it does receive, keeping its temperature change tiny

items.reveal_title: Mass times specific heat = thermal inertia
items.reveal:
A 1 kg piece of red-hot iron at 1300°C contains about 580 kJ above ambient. Strike it once on a 100 kg anvil and transfer (very roughly) a few percent of that heat by contact. The anvil — 100 kg with specific heat 460 J/kg·K — warms by maybe 0.2°C.

Multiple strikes can heat parts of the anvil noticeably but it dissipates fast through the anvil's mass and into the ground via its sturdy base. Anvils last decades of professional use without damage.

The principle generalises: heat sinks on CPUs, heat reservoirs in steam plants, and the oceans' role as Earth's thermal flywheel all rely on the same mass-times-heat-capacity logic.
items.why: Heat is taught with single-substance examples. Real heat transfer is set by mass, specific heat, contact area and time — not just temperature difference.

items.title: Bartlett made the first noble gas compound in 1962
items.claim: Until 1962 every chemistry textbook said noble gases were entirely unreactive. Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed that O2's ionisation energy (1175 kJ/mol) almost matches xenon's (1170). PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2. So PtF6 should be able to oxidise xenon. He tried it. XePtF6 formed instantly.
items.prompt: Why did this single result change inorganic chemistry?

options.text: It broke the assumed inviolability of the noble-gas 'rule of full octets' and opened the chemistry of an entire group of elements that had been written off as inert

items.reveal:
Bartlett's noticed PtF6 (a deep red solid) turned air red on contact: PtF6 had oxidised O2 to O2+ PtF6-. He looked up xenon's ionisation energy, saw the near-equality with O2, and reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise xenon.

The synthesis (Vancouver, March 1962) used a gas-handling apparatus he had built himself. Within months, Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating xenon with fluorine at 400°C.

Today: XeF2, XeF4, XeF6, XeO3, XeO4, KrF2, ArF (the last only at cryogenic temperatures). Bartlett died in 2008. His insight made the chemistry of noble gases a real subject overnight.
items.why: Chemistry has 'laws' that turn out to be untested generalisations. A single decisive experiment can break a 70-year consensus.
